articles.title: Agent of author Steven Galloway says sex assault allegations derailed promising career
articles.summary: The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been "impossible" to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault…

image.caption: Writer Steven Galloway is pictured in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. The former UBC creative writing professor's agent said unproven sexual assault allegations derailed Galloway's career during proceedings for a defamation trial. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been "impossible" to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author a decade ago.
Galloway alleges defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault

Henry Dunow described what he viewed as the detrimental impact of the claims on Galloway's "promising" career during a B.C. Supreme Court hearing in the author's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and other defendants.
Dunow said he thought of Galloway as a literary "star" with a bright future ahead.
But the allegations, which emerged in 2015, derailed that trajectory, he said.
Galloway has filed the lawsuit against a woman known only as A.B. and multiple others. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
An author's "social capital" and platform carry great importance in the industry, in a way more than the words on the page, Dunow told Monday's hearing.
Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the University of B.C., denies the allegations, and he was never charged.
He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose claims of rape and assault were found unsubstantiated by a former judge hired by the university.

items: 'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues
Author Steven Galloway finishes testifying at defamation trial

blocks.text: The lawsuit alleges A.B. and other defendants defamed Galloway by publishing the unproven allegations online and through other forums.
Several people originally named as defendants have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins
The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.
The woman, whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.
Galloway, the author of The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist, was fired by the university and has said his career was destroyed by the allegations.
He testified earlier this month that he could no longer write, his income from book royalties had "cratered" and he was selling boats for a living.

Dunow told Monday's hearing that the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective, meant to be a playful departure from his earlier, serious works.

He later agreed during cross-examination by A.B.'s lawyer Arden Beddoes that The Confabulist hadn't met expectations following the success of The Cellist of Sarajevo, though he said a so-called "sophomore slump" was not uncommon.

items: Steven Galloway testifies that faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program were common
Author tells B.C. defamation trial sexual assault claim derailed career, ability to write

blocks.text: The New York-based agent said he believed A.B.'s allegations had also thwarted the realization of a film option of The Cellist of Sarajevo dating back to around 2011.
The case has drawn intense attention in the Canadian literary scene.
A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway's case.
The court has previously heard that Galloway and A.B. had a two-year affair, which he has said ended in 2013.
Galloway testified she was a former student who was older than him, whom he'd met sometime in 2011 when she took a writing course from a colleague of his.

"I remain ashamed of having had an affair, period, let alone an affair with a student at the university I was at," he told an earlier hearing. "I should not have been cheating on my wife, and I should have not been doing it with a student."
A.B.'s former husband testified last week, called as a witness by Galloway's lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in the Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.'s ex-husband saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway's office, was like the "Aha!" moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

articles.title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.summary:
Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’

The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General,…

blocks.text: The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardian investigation published last December.
“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” said the 95-page legal complaint.

“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”
The lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.

The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.
Dollar General did not respond to questions for this story, but has previously said that it was “committed to providing customers with accurate prices on items purchased in our stores”.

The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025 investigation, which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.

The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.
“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”
The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”

Dollar General told the Guardian in 2025 that it is “disappointed” any time it fails to deliver on its commitment to accurate shelf pricing. In court documents in Ohio, Dollar General’s lawyers have argued that “it is virtually impossible for a retailer to match shelf pricing and scanned pricing 100% of the time for all items. Perfection in this regard is neither plausible nor expected under the law.”

In a statement accompanying the FTC lawsuit, the federal agency noted that Dollar General markets itself as a low-cost alternative to other retailers, and that low- and fixed-income customers rely on the accuracy of its price labels.

“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s bureau of consumer protection.

In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James, announced earlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.

articles.title: Hamilton and Niagara awaiting results as polls now closed

image.caption: Rick McRae cast his vote at Prince Philip Public School in Niagara Falls on Monday. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)

blocks.text: A voting sign is seen outside Hamilton city hall.
(Justin Chandler/CBC)
The Latest

items: Polls are now closed across Hamilton and Niagara, and results are expected to start rolling in shortly.
Hamilton has 13 mayoral candidates, including incumbent Andrea Horwath, Keanin Loomis, who came in a close second in 2022, and councillor Rob Cooper.
There are three open races for councillor in Hamilton (wards 8, 10 and 13) and four open races for mayor in Niagara (Welland, Thorold, Lincoln and Niagara-on-the-Lake).
You can find live results for the Hamilton mayoral race here.

October 27'They've got to keep up with the infrastructure,' Niagara voter saysRick McRae cast his vote at Prince Philip Public School in Niagara Falls on Monday. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)Rick McRae of Niagara Falls said after casting his vote that he wants action on what he sees as a growing homelessness and addictions problem. Property tax levels are a "big concern" to him, and he is particularly concerned about what he sees as not enough investments into critical infrastructure and roads."They’ve got to keep up with the infrastructure," he said. "My street has had four or five water main breaks just in the last couple of years. They put off work for so many years. You just can’t keep filling in the potholes."

How the CBC News Decision Desk makes its projectionsAndrew DavidsonHello. I'm a senior producer with the CBC News Decision Desk, a team of journalists who monitor results reporting on Election Night with the goal of making projections. Why? So we can give the audience as clear a sense of who will run their cities and communities as soon as possible. We study historical trends and consume the entirety of news coverage on election campaigns, including tips from our reporters on the ground. When the results start coming in, we watch for advance ballots and day-of votes to report, and we monitor how much the lead for one candidate grows. When we see enough separation and are comfortable with the state of the race, we can make a projection. But we don't elect people; voters do. Municipal elections generally present more of a challenge than provincial and federal votes, since there's usually less polling information available on individual races. Sometimes, the races are too close to call, and we must wait for the results to go final.We take our time to get it right. A late night just means more candy and snacks for us. We count votes on election night, not calories.

Polls close in Hamilton and Niagara municipal electionsEva SalinasHi, I'm Eva Salinas, executive producer of CBC Hamilton, here at our newsroom. The polls have now closed. City staff told us recently that they hope the first results will start appearing around 9 p.m., although the timing will depend on how quickly polling stations finish voting and report their results. We will be bringing results as soon as we have them here. You can also find live results of the mayoral race in Hamilton here.

October 26What voter turnout looked like in 2022Jeffery TramVoter turnout in the 2022 municipal election was 35.38 per cent, with 143,375 ballots cast out of 405,288 eligible voters. Although the turnout percentage fell compared to 2018, the number of voters was higher than the previous election and the highest total since 2000, according to the City of Hamilton.Peter Graefe, a professor in McMaster University's department of political science, told CBC Hamilton he is concerned fewer people may be following this election than last time. "It's hard to know whether Hamiltonians really know there's an election going on beyond the signs," he said.Karen Bird, another McMaster politics expert, said she worries about voter engagement this election, particularly among young people.

More than 30,000 people voted in Hamilton before todayJeffery TramA voting sign outside St. Thomas More Catholic Secondary School in Hamilton's Ward 14. (Saira Peesker/CBC)We're expecting most voting to take place today, but thousands of people have already cast their ballots.The City of Hamilton says 34,996 people voted during the first three weeks of advance voting, including 15,632 over the weekend of Oct. 17 and 18. That exceeds the 30,893 ballots cast over four days of advance voting in 2022. The numbers are reflective of the city's efforts to expand its options for voting ahead of election day. This includes a ballot-on-demand service that allows eligible voters to cast a ballot from a location regardless of which ward they live in. Ballots cast at advance polls and ballot-on-demand locations will be counted today.

Polling day 'snuck up on us,' voter says of a low-profile election seasonJustin ChandlerJonathan Deveau cast his ballot at Dr. J. E. Davey Elementary School on Monday election night in Hamilton. (Carlos Osorio/CBC)Jonathan Deveau, 42, voted in downtown Hamilton around 7:30 p.m. He said crime and homelessness were top of mind for him this election. He said didn’t hear many people talking about the election. "It felt like it snuck up on us."

Some candidates are already acclaimedJustin ChandlerSome candidates win before anyone even votes. That's called acclamation, and it's the process that happens when a candidate is the only one running for an elected office and wins by default. In Hamilton, more than a third of school board trustees were acclaimed, with one saying a shortage of candidates "isn't healthy for democracy."On the Hamilton-Wentworth District School Board, candidates for two of 11 seats won by acclamation:Incumbent Abby Zaitley in Ward 4.In Ward 13 Chris Slye was acclaimed when Andrea Wappel's name was withdrawn.At the Hamilton-Wentworth Catholic District School Board, candidates for four of the nine seats won by acclamation:Mark Valvasori, who was acclaimed in 2022, was again acclaimed for wards 1, 2 and 15.Ralph Agostino was acclaimed in wards 3 and 4.Incumbent Aldo D'Intino was acclaimed in Ward 5.In wards 9 and 11, current Ward 7 trustee Tyler Iorio was acclaimed.Nathalie Dufour Seguin was acclaimed for the French Catholic board trustee seat.The French public board trustee seat went to Sonia Macaluso, after the only other candidate, Pierre Gregory, withdrew.The eight acclamations on the school boards was four times higher than in 2022.The Association of Municipalities of Ontario said there were 400 candidate acclamations across the province in 2026, down from 548 in 2022 and 477 in 2018.

How will votes be counted?Jeffery TramWhen polls close at 8 p.m. in Hamilton, anyone still in line will be eligible to vote. Election workers will identify the end of the line and allow everyone present to finish voting before closing up.Throughout the day, workers feed marked ballots into a tabulator, which record votes. Paper ballots will be dropped into secure boxes.At the end of the day, the tabulators will print results showing the votes recorded by each machine.It is then sent to a central location, where the city will then start posting the results.Some polling locations experienced delays during the 2022 municipal election because of problems with software used to manage the voters' list. The system's servers slowed down, making it harder for staff to process voters quickly, the city has told us. This year, the city has an offline version of the software it can switch to if needed, along with backup internet connections and IT staff assigned to every ward.

Exciting races to watch across the regionJustin ChandlerBurlington city hall is seen in 2025. (Kate Bueckert/CBC)Had your fill of Hamilton's hot mayoral race? Things are nearly just as spicy in neighbouring Burlington, where two incumbent councillors — Lisa Kearns and Rory Nisan — are challenging the incumbent mayor, Marianne Meed Ward. With three of six sitting councillors not running for re-election, that city is sure to see new faces in the council chamber. There are at least three new Hamilton city councillors heading to city hall, as wards 8, 10 and 13 are without incumbents. In Ward 8, residents will get their third councillor in just over a year, as Rob Cooper is running for mayor instead of the council seat. In Ward 10, 11 candidates vying to replace Jeff Beattie, who ran and won a recent provincial byelection, becoming an MPP. And, in Ward 13, four candidates are facing off to replace Alex Wilson, who opted not to run again. Brantford is guaranteed to get a new mayor, with incumbent Kevin Davis not running again. There are seven candidates in that race, including three city councillors, a business owner and a wrestler. The mayor of Norfolk County, Amy Martin, also chose not to run again. There, seven candidates are running for mayor. And, in Haldimand County, three challengers are trying to beat the incumbent mayor, Shelley Ann Bentley.

This election sees a big change in NiagaraPaul ForsythA collage of election sign clusters along roadways in Niagara Falls. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)I'm Paul Forsyth, a CBC News reporter based in Niagara. I'll be watching what's shaping up to be some interesting election races in this region.One of the biggest changes is there are no choices for regional council for the first time in 56 years, because the Ontario government is eliminating the 19 region-only council positions. That means only the 12 Niagara mayors will sit on regional council, along with a provincially-appointed chair.Thorold, Niagara-on-the-Lake and Lincoln are all guaranteed to get new mayors because their incumbent mayors didn't run for re-election.The same is true in Welland, which has the hottest mayoral race. Eight people are vying to claim the seat left vacant by outgoing Mayor Frank Campion. In smaller Wainfleet, there's even a grudge match: former mayor Kevin Gibson, who was narrowly defeated in 2022 by current Mayor Brian Grant, is the sole challenger to Grant in this election.

articles.title: England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or
articles.summary: The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

image.caption: Kane, who is 33 years old, hails from London and is considered one of the greatest football players in the world Image: Franck Fife/AFP

blocks.text: England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.
The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.
The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.
The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.
Why did Harry Kane win the 2026 Ballon d'Or?
Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.
The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

blocks.caption: Harry Kane also received the Gerd Müller Trophy, awarded to the season's top goalscorer, after netting 73 goals for Bayern Munich and EnglandImage: Matthew Childs/Action Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.
At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.
"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.
Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.
"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

blocks.caption: Barcelona's Lamine Yamal was among Harry Kane's strongest rivals for the Ballon d'Or, alongside Kylian MbappeImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."
Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.
He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.
Who else won at the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards?
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.
The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

blocks.caption: Spain's Alexia Putellas won the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her careerImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.
She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.
Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.
Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.
Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

blocks.caption: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente beat Arsenal's Mikel Arteta and Aston Villa's Unai Emery to win the men's Coach of the Year awardImage: Franck Fife/AFP

blocks.text: Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.
Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

articles.title: Bato dela Rosa's wife Nancy thanks supporters, says he is not enemy
articles.summary: Nancy dela Rosa, wife of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, on Monday thanked her husband's supporters and said he is not the enemy of his friends and of the country.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 7:04am Updated October 27, 2026 7:12am
Nancy dela Rosa, wife of Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, on Monday thanked her husband's supporters and said he is not the enemy of his friends and of the country.
"Thank you for helping me realize that there are millions who still believe and support him," Nancy said in a post on Facebook.
"I just pray that the powerful few who were also his friends would come to realize he is not their enemy nor the enemy of this state," she said.
Nancy also appealed to those in power not to use Bato for their personal agenda.
"Pls do not use him for your personal agenda. He has helped you in countless ways and he has done you no wrong personally. He needs your help, not your persecution," she added.

Bato is in hiding after the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant of arrest for him on November 6, 2025 in connection with the crimes against humanity case involving former President Rodrigo Duterte.

He is charged before the ICC as a co-perpetrator with Duterte for cases of murder and attempted murder tied to the war on drugs of the latter's administration. Dela Rosa was the Philippine National Police (PNP) chief during the height of the Duterte administration’s bloody drug war campaign.
Both Duterte and Dela Rosa have denied the allegations against them.
Bato showed up at the Senate last May and was able to evade operatives who tried to implement the ICC arrest warrant.
He was thereafter placed under the protective custody of the Senate.
However, he was able to slip out of the Senate by riding with Senator Robin Padilla in the latter's vehicle.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government raised a P50-million reward this month for the arrest of Bato, who, according to Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla, is now considered "armed and dangerous."
Malacañang on Wednesday called on Bato to turn himself in and face the arrest warrant issued against him by the ICC so that a potentially violent confrontation could be prevented.
The Law Firm of Torreon and Partners has questioned the basis of the P50-million reward the DILG has offered for the arrest of Bato.

“The only document the government has is a warrant from the International Criminal Court. That is a foreign tribunal under a treaty the Philippines withdrew from effective March 17, 2019. No Philippine judge has examined that warrant, adopted it, or issued one of his own,” the firm said on Facebook.
“A reward system built on Philippine warrants cannot be used for a person who has no Philippine warrant,” it added.

Senators from the minority bloc on Saturday urged President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and concerned agencies to negotiate with the legal team of Bato for a “peaceful resolution” amid efforts to bring him before the ICC.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson said no violence should occur when Bato is arrested.
Remulla has said Bato is in Mindanao under the protection of a group with which authorities were seeking to negotiate his turnover.
The DILG chief explained that law enforcement officers could not simply move in to arrest the senator without risking a violent confrontation.

“In exchange for up to 10,000 potential deaths, I would rather negotiate first than cost the lives of Filipinos in this,” Remulla said. “You don’t always solve problems with a hammer. Sometimes you solve things better in a more peaceful, humane way.”
Remulla did not explain how he arrived at the figure or what basis he had for his estimate. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports
articles.summary:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil…

blocks.text: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title: Zalameda’s promises as chief justice bet: Solve case delays, more benefits for court staff
articles.summary: 'We have to gain the trust of the people in the domain of justice. I want a Supreme Court which is being seen by the people as their last bastion,' Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda says

blocks.text: FOR CJ. Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda during the Judicial and Bar Council's public interview for chief justice on Monday, October 26.
Supreme Court of the Philippines
'We have to gain the trust of the people in the domain of justice. I want a Supreme Court which is being seen by the people as their last bastion,' Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda says

items: Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda aims to prioritize the welfare of court employees and address disparities in benefits if appointed as the next Chief Justice of the Philippines.
He plans to tackle case backlogs by building more courthouses, utilizing technology for efficiency, and ensuring equitable distribution of cases among judges based on complexity.
Zalameda emphasizes the importance of collegiality within the Supreme Court and advocates for transparency in the judiciary to build public trust and minimize corruption.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda says he knows the plight of ordinary employees so he intends to focus on their welfare – among other innovations in the judiciary – should he become the country’s 28th Chief Justice.

“After passing the Bar in 1988, I began my career as a branch clerk of court of the Regional Trial Court of Makati. This gave me an appreciation of the challenges faced by our court employees,” Zalameda said during his public interview with the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) on Monday, October 26.

“The Judiciary is often spoken of in terms of judges, justices, decisions, and jurisprudence. But behind every decision are countless employees who perform their duties quietly and without recognition. I understand their challenges because I have been where many of them are,” he said.
Zalameda is one of the five candidates for chief justice, vying to replace Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will retire on November 6.

The aspiring chief justice currently holds seat No. 7 at the High Court. After serving for years at the Court of Appeals, he was appointed to the Supreme Court (SC) by then-president Rodrigo Duterte in August 2019.

After the public interviews, the JBC will send a short list of nominees to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who has the power to make the appointment. If chosen, Zalameda will serve for around seven years or until 2033.

During the Monday interview, JBC members asked Zalameda how much would be a workable budget for him if he is ever appointed as chief justice. He said any increase in the Court’s budget “will be greatly appreciated.”

They then asked him, if given additional funds, what would be his top priorities. Zalameda said he will focus on building additional courthouses to address delays in dispensing cases, using technology for more efficient processes, and increasing the benefits of judiciary employees.

“The judiciary must also confront delays that continue to burden litigants. I recognize that not all cases require the same amount of time and effort. We must consider their nature and complexity, the number of parties and witnesses, the volume of evidence, the length of proceedings, and the issues that must be resolved,” he said.
Zalameda also explained that there’s a discrepancy between the benefits that appellate court employees and lower courts employees receive. He said a study should be done to look into this disparity.

“I just want to cite an example: There is a perennial problem here with respect to the discrepancy between the allowances given to the appellate court employees and those in the trial courts. There was a time that the difference was I think more than 50%,” the aspiring chief magistrate explained.
“I think we have to review this and if we could get some funds…to supplement their budget for their allowances. That would be a good idea,” he added.

Zalameda said he strongly believes in separation of powers, and that each branch of the government — executive, legislature, and the judiciary — is by bound by its own constitutional mandate. He explained that he is a follower of the Constitution and always follows his conscience.
For him, a chief justice must be a servant of the judiciary and should work with litigants, lawyers, court staff, judges, and with fellow justices.

“The role is to create an environment where problems are heard, solutions are developed, good ideas are supported, and people are given the tools to fulfill their responsibilities. Leadership is ultimately about service, accountability, and enabling others to succeed,” Zalameda said.
As the chief magistrate, Zalameda said he also intends to lead with collegiality. He said he will respect his fellow members of the SC en banc.

“Collegiality does not mean the absence of disagreement. It means we can disagree without becoming disagreeable, and remain, after the debate and the vote, members of one Court serving one Constitution. This is the kind of collegiality I hope to strengthen – one built on mutual respect, professional trust, and a shared commitment to the institution,” said Zalameda.

To address case backlogs, apart from building more courthouses, Zalameda said there should be equal distribution of cases among judges based not on quantity, but based on the nature of the case, their complexity, and the parties involved. The justice said he will launch a study to address this matter.
The Office of the Court Administrator could be the office assigned for this, he explained.
Zalameda said he also believes that courts should be more transparent to minimize graft and corruption.

“We have to minimize also graft and corruption and the trust of the court should be established so that we can have later on high respect for the nation,” he explained. “I think we have to gain the trust of the people in the domain of justice. I want Supreme Court which is being seen by the people as their last bastion.”
He also explained that his judicial philosophy — the principle that guides him in deciding cases — is legal pragmatism. Zalameda said he believes that decisions should have real-life impact.

“In this principle of first prudence, you use the law as a tool to decide on cases, but we have to consider the realities, the cause and effect, that may result, and the effect on the people with respect to the decision which we made,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump administration tries to prosecute former FBI director James Comey for 3rd time
articles.summary: Former FBI director ‌James Comey is facing a third criminal case from ​U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, ​accusing him of sharing sensitive ​national security information, according to…

image.caption: Former director of the FBI James Comey speaks at Harvard University in February 2020. The Trump administration is trying for a third time to prosecute Comey for disclosing classified information. (Charles Krupa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Former FBI director ‌James Comey is facing a third criminal case from ​U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, ​accusing him of sharing sensitive ​national security information, according to court documents ‌made public on Monday.
Word of new case comes same day judge rules administration illegally fired his daughter

The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute former FBI director James Comey for what it calls disclosing classified information, employing the unusual manoeuver of bypassing a grand jury — a move Comey's lawyers say makes the case legally invalid.
The allegations from the U.S. Justice Department came in documents unsealed Monday in federal court in Washington.

It would be the third criminal case that the Justice Department has brought against the longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump since the Republican president's return to the White House last year.

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."
The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a criminal information to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case.

"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.

The new ‌case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening Trump in ​a social media post.
A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats ⁠case remains pending.
Trump wanted pledge of loyalty

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-president Barack Obama, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.

A judge ruled Monday that Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, seen here in May 2025, was illegally fired by the Trump administration from her position as assistant U.S. attorney. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president — an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.
News of the new case against Comey came the same day a judge ruled the Trump administration illegally fired Comey's daughter, Maurene, as a Justice Department prosecutor.
With files from CBC News and Reuters

articles.title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
articles.summary:
Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes

  • Get our

blocks.text: The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest against school underfunding, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.
Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis as households grapple with high and rising prices.
The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude but the grievances are common.

Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.
Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.
More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.

France’s high public debt, stagnant economy and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.
France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.
Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.
Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.
“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.
“It’s a warning signal.”

Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.

“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.
The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.
after newsletter promotion

In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.
“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.
“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”
President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.
“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.
The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.

France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.
That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.

Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.

“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”

While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.
“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”

articles.title: Massachusetts lesbian bar makes frantic effort to find new owners after relaxing masking policy
articles.summary:
Last Ditch bar announced it would ‘soft close’ after it went viral following a story on its attempt to relax Covid rules

A Massachusetts lesbian bar that went viral for loosening its Covid…

blocks.text: A Massachusetts lesbian bar that went viral for loosening its Covid mask policy last month announced plans to “soft close” on Monday as it seeks new ownership.

The Last Ditch bar, in the small city of Greenfield, said in an Instagram post that it was searching for co-owners, new owners or a full sale, and that it would “soft close effective immediately”, with “only booked events” continuing while it closes this winter. It had opened just last year as a bar for “dykes, transsexuals, gender freaks, workers, and their friends”.

Last month the bar went viral following a Boston Globe story documenting a masking dispute after the owners attempted to relax the bar’s Covid mask-wearing policy for one night a week in a bid to drive up Saturday business. The bar had been struggling to raise revenue while adhering to a strict policy of mask-wearing, but the proposed change prompted a backlash from customers who accused the owners of ableism and abandoning immunocompromised people.
There was then a backlash to those critics, with people piling on and mocking customers’ concerns about contracting Covid.

The publicity did also attract some support to the bar, but evidently, not enough. “We put our lives on hold to foster networks of care, resources and a home base for organizing. It’s time we pass it on,” the bar said on Instagram.

“We’ve been fighting since the beginning to fill out the team, and we still don’t have a board/leadership to manage workers’ owned co-op transfer. We are soft closing effective immediately; all booked events will continue; otherwise, we are closed.”
In seeking new ownership, the bar noted that the sale would include the furniture, equipment, inventory and social media pages, to an estimated value of $70,000.

As set out in the Globe’s article, the bar was already in financial trouble before the masking furor, and two of the three original owners had dropped out of the project. The remaining owner was left with the responsibility of repaying the $50,000 loan the three took out to open the bar and was living out of her truck and working several jobs to try to keep it running.
The Guardian has reached out to the Last Ditch bar for comment.

articles.title: Carers allowed to earn over the weekly limit without losing out as ‘cliff-edge’ abolished in the budget
articles.summary:
Controversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigation

The controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with…

blocks.text: The controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.

The chancellor, John Healey, is to announce a new digital taper system for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s budget, effectively ending what is regarded as one of the UK benefit system’s most feared and unfair administrative practices.

The scandal was highlighted in a Guardian investigation that revealed how hundreds of thousands of carers have, through no fault of their own, run up life-changing debts in recent years after overstepping weekly earnings thresholds by just a few pence.

Those hefty debts were then ruthlessly chased down by welfare officials who pursued carers using legislation designed to recover funds from drug dealers and organised crime bosses. Some unpaid carers were convicted of fraud as a result.

The cliff-edge rule dictates that if a carer earns even a penny more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – they forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, currently £86.45. A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40.
Although the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) was aware when carers breached earnings limits, it refused to warn them, insisting the onus was on carers to report any changes.
Thousands of carers spent long periods unaware of the breach, in some cases for years, resulting in overpayment debts typically of £2-£5,000 but in some cases as much as £20,000.

Under new rules set to be announced in the budget, the introduction of a tapered system instead of a cliff-edge means only £1 of carer’s allowance will be removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit, meaning carers are no longer left financially worse off for working additional hours or receiving a pay rise.

The announcement is one of five more “everyday fixes” announced by Healey ahead of his budget on Wednesday. His room for manoeuvre is severely constrained by the tight fiscal backdrop, a result of global events including the conflict in Iran.

Treasury insiders have warned that the budget will be low-key, with difficult tax and spend decisions put off until the spending review next year. But there is anxiety among some Labour MPs over the scale of the announcements, after Andy Burnham came to power promising major change.

Among the other measures to come is making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent – with the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles locked in, and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p per mile. The Treasury said the move would benefit about 3 million people – employees and self-employed – who use their own vehicle for work.

The chancellor’s intervention on the draconian cliff-edge rule comes after an award-winning Guardian investigation which revealed how the DWP had for years known of the profound distress it caused carers – including warnings from a DWP whistleblower – but did nothing about it.

The Guardian’s reporting triggered a government-commissioned independent review of carer’s allowance overpayments by disability rights expert Liz Sayce, published last year. It found unpaid carers suffered depression and hardship on a huge scale after falling foul of a series of systemic injustices, including the cliff edge.

In one case highlighted by the review, a carer was penalised when the national minimum wage had increased at a faster rate than the earnings limit. This put her 15p a week above the limit, even though her hours had not changed. Months later, she was told she had incurred a £2,000 penalty for above-limit earnings totalling just £5.

The review found the outdated design of carer’s allowance, coupled with longstanding DWP failures in its administration, meant about 180,000 carers ran up overpayment debts amounting to £300m between 2019 and 2025.

Campaigners welcomed the decision, calling it a “long-overdue reform” although there was disappointment the technical demands of building a new digital system to run the taper means it will not be introduced before the end of the decade.

Carers UK said the cliff-edge plays havoc with carers’ attempts to work part-time around their minimum 35 hours a week of caring duties, with many giving up paid work or refusing promotions, overtime or bonuses because of the risks.

John Healey, the chancellor, told the Guardian the carer’s allowance system had worked against carers. “That means doing an extra shift or getting a small pay rise can actually leave someone worse off. That cannot be right.

“So at this budget on Wednesday, we’re ending that cliff-edge. Carer’s allowance will instead taper as earnings increase, giving carers the freedom to work a little more and earn a little more without suddenly losing all their support.”

As well as unpaid carers, Healey’s budget will benefit an extra 150,000 new parents – including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out – with parental support worth up to £194 a week.

Ministers are also removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on paraffin.
There will also be hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, to make it more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue.

Healey will also reportedly raise the minimum wage by about 4% to about £13.20 an hour. However, in a sign of government concern over rates of youth unemployment, the chancellor is said to be about to raise youth rates by roughly the same amount, rather than the inflation-busting levels seen in previous budgets.

Labour came to office in 2024 promising to raise the youth rate, which applies to workers under 21, to the same level as the full rate. But ministers have become concerned in recent months that raising the minimum wage for younger workers could be dissuading companies from taking on young employees.
“We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair,” Burnham said.

“If you’re a nurse driving to work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket.”

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “We have listened to [carers’] concerns about the cliff-edge built into the system which leaves them financially worse off for taking on a few more hours, or getting a modest pay rise, and intend to bring that to an end.”
Kirsty McHugh, chief executive of Carers Trust, said: “It is great news that the government is acting to remove the carer’s allowance cliff-edge. This is an important and long-overdue reform.
“We would urge the government to use this change as a springboard for a wider and deeper reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit that remains stuck in the 1970s and must be made fit for the future.”

Emily Holzhausen, Carers UK director of policy, said: “We have countless stories from carers who have shared their deep fears of going just a few pence over the earnings limit and losing all of their benefit.

“It’s absolutely right that the chancellor is thinking of practical changes that will make their lives easier. A taper on the earnings limit should give families much more choice about working and still caring.”

articles.title: Trump dangles $1m reward for reporting voter fraud in past or upcoming elections
articles.summary:
President’s comments come ahead of November midterm elections and follow his claims of widespread voter fraud

Donald Trump has

blocks.text: Donald Trump has announced a $1m reward for reports of voter fraud in past elections and the upcoming midterm elections, with payment contingent on the arrest and conviction of those responsible.

In a Truth Social post on Monday, the president wrote: “Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump later reiterated the offer to reporters before boarding Air Force One for a campaign rally in Mississippi, saying: “I’m also going to be issuing a $1m bonus or reward, or whatever you want to call it, for anybody that reports voter fraud, leading to the arrest and conviction of somebody.”
Trump did not disclose how he plans to pay for the rewards.
The Guardian has reached out to the White House for comment.
Trump’s latest comments come ahead of the November midterm elections and follow his repeated and unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

Earlier this month, Democratic state attorneys general expanded coordination efforts to counter potential federal interference in the upcoming elections, amid growing concerns over the administration’s voter fraud claims.
California’s attorney general Rob Bonta criticized the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict alleged noncitizen voting, accusing it of “politicizing and weaponizing the law”.

In 2020, Texas’s Republican lieutenant governor Dan Patrick offered a $25,000 for election-fraud tips, saying at the time: “I support President Trump’s efforts to identify voter fraud in the presidential election and his commitment to making sure that every legal vote is counted and every illegal vote is disqualified.”

Following Patrick’s offer, the first payout went to Eric Frank, a Democratic poll worker in Pennsylvania whose tip led to the conviction of a 72-year-old Republican for voting twice – once in his own name and once in his son’s – the Washington Post reported in 2021.

articles.title: Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after deadly church attack
articles.summary: Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.

image.caption: Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects related to the terrorist attack on the Hammoud Church in Karak GovernorateImage: Alaa Al-Sukhni/REUTERS

blocks.text: Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.
Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.
Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.
But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.
A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.
Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province
Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.

blocks.caption: King Abdullah II (center) visited victims in hospital and called for Jordanian security forces to respond with an "iron fist."Image: Royal Court of Jordan/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

articles.title: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack
articles.summary:
Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak

Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for…

blocks.text: Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.

It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.

Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.

Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.

In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.

Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.
The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.

Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.
The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.

“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.
Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.
“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.
Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.

“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.
“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.
But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”

articles.title: The U.S. put surveillance drones in the Great Lakes, and this border town mayor isn't happy
articles.summary: When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of…

image.caption: Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley says he was not informed about plans for the U.S. Coast Guard to put drones on the Great Lakes. (CBC News)

blocks.text: As It Happens

When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard.
'We have thousands of boaters,' says Sarnia, Ont., mayor. 'They're going to be photographed and watched'
When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars."

Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard to "gather critical weather data for emergency response planning, track illicit activity and keep maritime borders safe."
The U.S. Coast Guard, which operates under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, told CBC in June the vessels aren't there to surveil Canadians. But Bradley isn't convinced.
"We have thousands of boaters on the river St. Clair, Lake Huron, Lake Erie, and now they're going to be photographed and watched," he told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"Even though they're saying right now it's benign, I don't have the trust down the road, especially with the rapidly deteriorating relationship with the U.S., that they won't use it for other purposes."
CBC has reached out to the U.S. and Canadian Coast Guards for comment. Both said they could not respond by deadline.
LISTEN | Interview with Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley :
As It Happens7:00Sarnia, Ont., mayor speaks out against U.S. surveillance drones in the Great Lakes
The vessels are called Voyager unmanned surface vehicles, and each one is affixed with 360-degree high-resolution cameras, advanced radar, and automatic identification systems.
They are owned and operated by Saildrone, a private U.S. company whose $15.5-million US contract with the Coast Guard is funded by U.S. President Donald Trump's "One Big, Beautiful Bill."

“This Voyager fleet will help the Coast Guard maintain persistent, scalable maritime domain awareness across these expansive waters, identifying threats in real time and enabling focused, high-impact interdiction," Saildrone president John Mustin said in a press release.
The U.S. Coast Guard now has two sail drones on Lake Erie as a part of a new program that launched in May. (U.S. Coast Guard)
York University researcher Petra Molnar says Canadians should be concerned that this data is being collected by a private company and sold to the U.S. government.

“This is a very troubling arrangement from a privacy and accountability standpoint," Molnar, the author of The Walls Have Eyes: Surviving Migration in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, told the Guardian newspaper.

"We have very little public information about data retention, who can access what data is collected, or how people using the region recreationally [can] be swept up in a data system built for border enforcement.”
Saildrone did not respond to requests for comment from CBC.

items: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
U.S. claims about higher drug trafficking from Canada don't match the data: fentanyl czar

blocks.text: The U.S. Coast Guard has said drones are nothing for Canadians to worry about.

"They're just out there for awareness," Lt. Junior Grade Samuel Rodriguez Garcia told CBC Windsor in June, when the vessels were deployed in Lake Erie. "Think of them as mobile cameras that kind of help us gain a better insight into what's going on live on scene."
He said the vessels' cameras are monitored 24/7 by U.S. Coast Guard staff, who can also manually move the drones when necessary. But the footage isn't recorded, officials say.
U.S. and Canadian agencies, including law enforcement, could have access to the drone technology after going through the proper channels, he said.
The Canadian Coast Guard told CBC Windsor it works closely with its U.S. counterpart, but has no involvement with the drone sail program.
Mayor says he was left in the dark
The U.S. Coast Guard first announced the Voyager project in May in a press release issued by the U.S. Department of War.
But Bradley says this is the first he's heard of it.
In fact, he says he only learned what the vessel in the St. Clair River was when he was contracted by the Detroit News, which has been reporting on the drones.
As mayor of the largest city on Lake Huron, he says being kept in the dark is unacceptable.
"If the Canadian government knew and agreed to it, that, to me, is a big issue," he said. "They should have let Canadian cities, Canadian mayors, know that this was happening."
CBC reached out to Public Safety Canada for information about the drones, and was redirected to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).
The CBSA did not respond to questions about Bradley's concerns, saying the RCMP is responsible for "enforcing Canadian legislation between ports of entry, including on the water."
The U.S. Coast Guard sail drones will be deployed in Lake Erie and be pulled from the water once ice forms. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Bradley says it's no coincidence the project comes during a period of heightened tension between Canada and the U.S.
With both countries locked in an impasse in the trade war, Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly framed the Canadian border as a dangerous security threat.
However, the numbers tell a different story. A U.S. Border Patrol officials told Congress in June that drug seizures and arrests of undocumented immigrants are both down along the U.S-Canada border.

items: Detroit tourism bureau halts advertising in Canada amid trade war, hopes Canadians won't 'hold grudge'
Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year

blocks.text: Bradley called the drones "an answer to a problem that doesn't really exist." He called on the Canadian government to "show some backbone" and push back.
"The Elbows Up movement seems to have died away, and I was a big supporter of that because I know the American psyche so well from 40 years of dealing with them," he said.
"If you don't stand up or push back they will just walk all over you."
Interview with Mike Bradley produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank
articles.summary:
Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces

An international delegation including British politicians has been…

blocks.text: An international delegation including British politicians has been barred from entering the West Bank on a trip to meet Palestinian children, farmers and society leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces during olive harvest season.

The delegation of 23 people, including four elected representatives, was drawn from countries including France, Spain, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, Holland, Ireland and the US. It included the Labour MP Clive Lewis, the Scottish National party MP Lara Bird, the Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens and the former Labour MP Sam Tarry.

Lewis told the Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. I use the word interrogated because people were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”

The delegates were set to participate in Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress, a gathering to oppose Israeli occupation in Palestine. The congress was organised by Progressive International in partnership with Birzeit University and includes a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations.

blocks.caption: Clive Lewis (left) and Sam Tarry were both denied entry to the West Bank at the border crossing checkpoint. Photograph: Global Justice Now

blocks.text: Tarry told the Guardian that he thought the delegation had a “genuine chance of going across” into the West Bank but they were detained at the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge by Israeli forces in Jordan for nine hours. “They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” he added.

The exclusions occurred amid attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and foreign press and activists in the region. International travel to parts of the West Bank is permitted but subject to military checkpoints. Earlier this month, Israeli media reported that the defence minister, Israel Katz, had instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists travelling to Palestinian olive-harvesting areas.

In the first two weeks of October, the UN aid coordination office recorded at least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest, often under the protection or with the participation of Israeli forces.

Israeli forces attacked European diplomats and a French mayor accompanying Palestinian farmers, while about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander, were also recently detained.
Bird said in a statement: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given.

“It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so. If Israel has nothing to hide, why is it so determined to stop us seeing what is happening in the occupied West Bank?”

Laila Hazaineh, a political coordinator for Progressive International, said in a statement: “Despite escalating violence, our delegation remained determined to cross to Palestine to participate in the olive harvest, and actively engage with Palestinian communities and institutions. Every refusal of entry will only strengthen this determination.”
The embassy of Israel has been contacted for comment.
