articles.title: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
articles.summary: Maurene Comey believes she was let go from her job as a federal prosecutor because her father is the former FBI director.

blocks.text: The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.

Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".

Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".

A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
articles.summary:
Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Julian Borger in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.

“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.

blocks.caption: An AI-generated image of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv was posted on Netanyahu’s X account on Sunday.  Photograph: X/Benjamin Netanyahu

blocks.text: Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.

In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, is the most likely challenger to Netanyahu as prime minister.  Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA

blocks.text: Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.

The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.

As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”

He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.

The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.

The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu has been emphasising in his campaign the support he has from Donald Trump. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

blocks.text: In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”

The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.

In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.

In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.

“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”

Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.

His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.

Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' trial hears recording of Aiden Pleterski admitting $300M fund 'never existed'
articles.summary: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski admitted his $300-million fund never existed in a June 2022 audio recording played in court at his fraud trial in Toronto on Monday.

blocks.text: 'Crypto King' admits $300M account never existed in audio recording played at trial
Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski admitted his $300-million fund never existed in a June 2022 audio recording played in court at his fraud trial in Toronto on Monday.

Pleterski, 27, was providing screenshots and videos of his FXChoice trading platform account with a balance more than $311 million to concerned investors just weeks before the recorded meeting with three investors, Pleterski and a lawyer he brought with him, Ontario Superior Court heard.
One of those three investors, Chris Winn, testified remotely.

The retired Durham Regional Police officer was the last of 14 witnesses the Crown called in their case, which wrapped Monday after Winn's testimony. The prosecution also withdrew the money laundering charge Pleterski was facing.

Winn, who invested a combined $450,000 himself and through a holding company, said he got back $330,000. He testified to attending two meetings with Pleterski at the Pickering, Ont., home of another investor.

Chris Winn, a retired Durham Regional Police officer, invested a combined $450,000 himself and through a holding company with Aiden Pleterski, and testified in Ontario Superior Court that he got back $330,000. (Monica Winn/Facebook)
"He told us basically he hadn't traded any of the money and basically it's a Ponzi scheme," said Winn.
Pleterski, who is representing himself at trial, pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and the now withdrawn money laundering charge.

items: 'Crypto King' spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies
Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest

blocks.text: Near the beginning of the roughly three-hour recording from the second meeting, this exchange between Pleterski and the two other investors present, Brad Rogers and Jason Affleck, occurs:
Pleterski: "The $300 million it was —"
Rogers: "Never existed, you said."
Pleterski: "It never existed."
Affleck: "But how was that shown to us on a screen, and a piece of paper, was that Photoshopped? Or was that documented? Like how was that — we saw it?"
Pleterski: "Mitch showed you the picture and all that based on whatever, then that account basically never existed."
Winn, a retired Durham Regional Police officer and one of Pleterski's investors, testified remotely at Pleterski's trial on Monday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Earlier in the trial, another investor and former friend of Pleterski's, Mitchell Learning, testified he went looking for "proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski's investment account — after receiving a screenshot and video showing the FX Choice with a $311-million balance.

Learning went to Pleterski's lakefront mansion in Burlington, Ont., in June 2022 and was able to access Pleterski's email account on his computer. He testified that he found an email from FXChoice confirming Pleterski had deleted that account.

items: 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn't exist

blocks.text: Learning told the court Pleterski admitted to losing the money trading the year before and said to Learning that he'd been paying investors back with other investors' funds since then.
Mitchell Learning outside Ontario Superior Court in Toronto on Oct. 9 at the trial of Pleterski. (Mehrdad Nazarahar/CBC)
The investor meeting with Winn, Pleterski and others took place about a week after Learning testified Pleterski confessed what was going on to Learning in June 2022, according to the recording.
"Since January, I've refunded $700,000, lost it, I've refunded $1 million, lost it, I've refunded $300,000, lost it," said Pleterski at the recorded meeting.
"That was money that was taken in from investors."
A couple of investors talking over each other say "from us" and "we paid all your debts."

Over the course of the meeting, the investors try to suggest that Pleterski liquidate his assets and put them into a business controlled by the investors. From there, they would supervise Pleterski conducting trades to make everyone's money back. They also regularly repeat they don't trust Pleterski because he's lied to them and make multiple references to him going to jail.
Police officers invested
"This is one of the biggest Ponzi schemes in f--king Ontario," said Winn, in one of those instances. "It'll be front page of the paper."

Winn and Affleck also get angry about the impact on other investors they know and who they introduced to Pleterski's operation. In one instance, Winn implies current Durham Regional Police officers invested with Pleterski.
"I got guys that still work at the police department all over this f--king list," said Winn in the recording.
"I retired as one of the f--king most well-liked respected guys that had rank, like a high rank. And they're going to be like 'what the f--ck?' "
Winn testified he retired from Durham police as a staff sergeant in 2020 after nearly 30 years with the service.
Pleterski enters Ontario Superior Court in Toronto on Oct. 5. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
Affleck describes how losing the investments will devastate "normal people" he knows.
"They've mortgaged their houses, they've got lines of credit," Affleck tells Pleterski at the recorded meeting.

"You've met these people, they're family, they're friends, they're f--king cleaning ladies. They're normal people that have worked their whole lives to work up to this money and you've taken it. That's why this is upsetting."
'I'm sitting here trying to make it right': Pleterski
After another part of the recording where investors talk about Pleterski lying, he raises his voice in response.
"If I had a malicious intent with any of this, I wouldn't be sitting in front of you guys, I'd be on a f--king plane getting out of here right now," said Pleterski.
"I could have been gone long, a long f--king time ago, but I'm sitting here trying to make it right. Everybody's f--king leaning on me."
In the recording, Pleterski also argued that he knows how to trade, but said that he wasn't in the headspace to do it well given the stress he's under.

Since the start of his trial in early October, the Crown has alleged that Pleterski guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds, instead spending the money on himself. Just over a week ago, the court was presented with the first detailed evidence in support of that aspect of the prosecution's case.
$16.3M spent on himself: accountant

A senior forensic accountant who reviewed Pleterski's financial records testified that investors provided Pleterski with more than $36.3 million and none of those funds were ever sent to FXChoice, the trading platform investor contracts said Pleterski would use on their behalf.

Instead, Albert Ciorma from the Ontario Securities Commission said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets and $598,000 on security.
Albert Ciorma, a senior forensic accountant with the Ontario Securities Commission, testified earlier this month in Pleterski's fraud trial. (Pam Davies/CBC)
Pleterski also gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents and took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card, Ciorma said.
Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million. Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.
Pleterski won't testify
After the Crown completed its case Monday, Justice Shaun Nakatsuru asked Pleterski whether he was going to call evidence or testify in his own defence.
"No, I don’t have the legal expertise to do so, your honour," replied Pleterski. "I don’t know what to ask or to say.”
Pleterski only cross-examined the first Crown witness at his trial.
Closing statements and the judge's charge to the jury are expected Wednesday.

articles.title: iPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handset
articles.summary:
Company says small number of devices affected by display glitch after posts appear on Reddit and social media

Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen,…

blocks.text: Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units.

Reports of cracks have emerged on Reddit and social media platforms since the handset went on general sale globally on Friday. Experts said there had been too few examples to determine whether there was a more serious problem with Apple’s first foldable device, which retails from $1,999 (£1,499).
Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch.

“We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said.
One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it and posted their experience on Reddit.

“I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen,” they wrote alongside an image of the phone showing an apparent display malfunction where a white strip of light ran along one half of the screen.
“As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.”

They said their local Apple store had replaced the phone immediately. The Guardian has been unable to verify the user’s claims. Another user in Australia posted that they had heard “almost a cracking noise” on their handset, which resulted in a similar screen malfunction.

blocks.caption: IPhone Duo handsets on display at an Apple store in London. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP

blocks.text: A report by the Bloomberg news service also highlighted similar issues among users in the US and India.
Apple believes the affected units are showing defects quickly after use. It said the response from early users had been “incredibly positive”.

The company said demand had been “nothing short of extraordinary” for the iPhone Duo, its most high-profile product launch under the company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
after newsletter promotion

The device has sold out and the next round of shipments is not expected until January, according to a report in the Economic Daily, a publication based in Taiwan, the home country of Foxconn, Apple’s main device manufacturer.

Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of data and analytics at IDC, a tech research company, said it was too early to tell whether the screen issue was significant. “This is quite common when a new product comes to market,” he said.

Citing similar problems at Samsung in 2019, he said: “What matters now is how the company responds … Samsung experienced problems with the original Galaxy Fold in 2019, but it also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category.
“Apple said that any customer with problems should ask for a replacement, which is the right first step.”

Ben Wood, the chief analyst at the research firm CCS, said he was taking a very cautious view of the Duo screen problem and that there was as yet no evidence of a more widespread issue with the device.

articles.title: Middle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister says
articles.summary:
Badr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of security

The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back…

blocks.text: The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.
Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.

He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.

blocks.caption: From left, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir, and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, at a meeting in Tehran on Monday. Photograph: Iranian Presidency Office/AP

blocks.text: Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.
Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.

Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.

He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.
“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”

He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.

He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”

blocks.caption: Badr Albusaidi, left, with Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in Tehran in August. Photograph: Iranian Foreign Ministry/AP

blocks.text: Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.

Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”

The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.

The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.
A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

articles.title: Police locate vehicle allegedly used by Toronto mother to abduct 3 children
articles.summary: Toronto police say they have found a vehicle believed to have been used to abduct three children from Scarborough on Friday, but the children and their mother have not been found.

image.caption: From left, Daniel, six, Irina, three, and four-month-old Anastasia. The three children were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when their mother took them and fled, according to police. (Toronto Police Service)

blocks.text: Toronto
Toronto police say they have found a vehicle believed to have been used to abduct three children from Scarborough on Friday, but the children and their mother have not been found.
Children, mother not yet found, police say
In a news release Monday, police said the mother of the three children, Somerda Miclescu, 22, was believed to be driving a 2017 White Ford Expedition vehicle with Ontario licence plate DJJS 875.
Police did not say where or when they found the vehicle.

Daniel, six, Irina, three, and Anastasia, four months, were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when polices say their mother took them and fled. Police say the children's mother does not have legal custody of them.
"Efforts to locate them remain ongoing," police said in the release.
Police described the mother as 5 feet 7 inches, about 180 pounds, with long, black hair. Police said she was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top.
Somerda Miclescu is wanted by police for allegedly abducting her three children. (Toronto Police Service)
Police first responded to a call at about 11:30 a.m. Friday for an abduction in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

items: Toronto police seeking mother, 22, for allegedly abducting her 3 children

blocks.text: Ionut Stroe, 25, the owner of the vehicle that Miclescu allegedly used to abduct the children, has been named by police as a person of interest in the case.
Stroe is also wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order, unrelated to the abduction.
Police described him as being around 5 feet 11 inches, 235 pounds, with a tattoo on his right forearm.

articles.title: Quebec's Spa Nordik introduces new safety measures following sexual assault allegations
articles.summary: Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., has announced new measures to protect clients amid a class action lawsuit alleging sexual assault that implicates 36 massage therapists who worked there over a…

image.caption: In a list outlined on its website, Spa Nordik says massage therapists will now undergo criminal background checks and get training on consent and the prevention of sexual violence. (Jean-Sébastien Marier/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa

Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., has announced new measures to protect clients amid a class action lawsuit alleging sexual assault that implicates 36 massage therapists who worked there over a 19-year period.
Background checks, consent forms, and security personnel among new steps
Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., has announced new measures to protect clients amid a class action lawsuit alleging sexual assault that implicates 36 massage therapists over a 19-year-period.
In a list outlined on its website, the spa says massage therapists will now undergo criminal background checks and get training on consent and the prevention of sexual violence.
They'll also be "required to maintain good standing with a recognized professional association."
Massage services will be relegated to their own floor with security personnel, the spa says.

items: Class action alleging sexual assaults at Spa Nordik to proceed

blocks.text: Other measures include an electronic consent form that clients will be able to update throughout their massage and a requirement for therapists to obtain consent before massaging "sensitive areas."
The spa defines those as the "buttocks [and] upper inner thighs" and the "pectoral area."
Clients will also have the option to have the audio of their session recorded. A new complaint process for clients is also being implemented, the spa says.
Founder 'deeply shaken'

In a statement shared on social media, Groupe Nordik founder Martin Paquette wrote that the company is committed to the safety of its clients, adding that he was "deeply shaken," and "angry" when he learned of the allegations.
"No one should ever have to go through something like that in a place dedicated to well-being," he wrote.
Paquette also called for stronger government oversight of Quebec's massage therapy sector.
"Unfortunately, what has happened at our establishment is not unique to Nordik," he said.

articles.title: Major clean-up under way after two storms cause havoc in Britain
articles.summary: More strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and flooding
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A major clean-up operation was under way on Monday after weekend storms caused havoc, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come.
Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms, Austen and Boelo, struck parts of the UK, and there was widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations.
The Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power on Monday morning. That figure was later down to 39,000.

The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread, with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend.
He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen,” he said.

Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northern Scotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc,” Slade said.

blocks.caption: Storm Boelo causes severe flooding in town centre of Largs, Scotland

blocks.text: The weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way and issued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times. The Met Office advised people to take care near cliffs and be aware of strong waves.

The second warning will be in place from 3am to 9pm on Tuesday and covers most of Scotland. Forecasters said winds of 50-60mph were likely to be quite widespread, with gusts up to 70mph in the far north. It warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and more power cuts.
The weekend storms led to two deaths, authorities said. A 60-year-old man was hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway, while a man in his 20s died in Finchley, north London.
The 60-year-old was named on Monday afternoon as Richard Baines, the curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Port Logan.

David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, said Baines would be remembered for his “passion and enthusiasm for plants … significantly increasing and expanding the plant collection at Logan”.

There was flooding in several parts of Scotland, with dramatic footage from Largs showing flood water cascading through the town centre. One resident said it was the highest she had ever seen in 36 years of living there.

Staff at the Thai restaurant Tha-Tien-Thai shared a video of their kitchen overrun by water with the desperate caption: “There is nothing left.” They said its doors would be closed for the foreseeable future “due to larger flood restoration than originally planned”.
Robyn Cryans, an executive assistant from Renfrew, is on holiday in Cyprus and woke to see pictures taken by a neighbour of her Nissan Micra Sport submerged back at home.

“It is very upsetting, a bit stressful,” she said. “It was unexpected considering we’ve got a £10m flood barrier literally just down the road which is supposed to activate if the Clyde bursts its banks.”

blocks.caption: A downed tree in Gladstone Park, London, on Sunday after strong winds overnight.  Photograph: Martin Evans/PA

blocks.text: She is scheduled to fly back on Tuesday and fully expects to find her flat damaged. “I’m obviously very upset about it, but at the end of the day it’s material objects. It could have been a lot worse.”
In Aberdeenshire, 13 primary schools without power were shut on Monday, and Ellon academy was closed because of storm damage. Ten primary schools were shut in the Highlands.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency teams and forecasters on Sunday to discuss the ongoing response to the weather.

Emergency services were called to a flooded care home in Saltcoats, North Ayrshire, on Sunday evening. Police Scotland said everyone at the care home was accounted for, road closures were in place and officers were expected to remain on site overnight to assist.

There was also travel disruption, with flights diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford, England’s highest airport, and others cancelled. Most train services were getting back to normal but operators advised customers to check before they travelled.

The storms brought a number of event cancellations including the Sunday racing at Aintree, abandoned because of the high winds. The Guardian’s live blog of the terrible tea-time Sunderland v Leeds goalless draw summed up the action: “And the winner is … the wind.”

articles.title: AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion
articles.summary: Anthropic has filed paperwork for an initial public offering that could be one of the biggest in history. The co-founders have outlined both the benefits and the risks of AI in their pitch to…

image.caption: Dario Amodei has addressed concerns about the development of the AI industryImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic on Monday filed paperwork to make its stock market debut in what analysts say could be one of the biggest in history.
The initial public offering (IPO) could happen as early as November, reports say, with analysts putting the company at a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
What did the Anthropic founders say about the IPO?
The seven co-founders of the company, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, outlined their vision for the future of AI in a letter to potential investors.
"We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," they said.

The AI startup behind Claude also addressed the societal risks of AI as they have done before, writing that the company's leadership might have to take unusual decisions to slow down the pace of development, even if that meant falling behind competitors.
The filing toward an IPO represents a major milestone for a company that was founded just five years ago.
Money raised at the IPO could provide the company with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated
What do we know about Anthropic's IPO?
Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."
But the company is yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell and what price, leaving that space blank in its paperwork filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.
Anthropic filed confidentially with the SEC in June and that gave the agency time to go over the company's financial credentials before they were made available to the public and potential investors.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters.
Anthropic debut follows SpaceX IPO
The San Francisco-based company was founded by members who defected from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2021.
OpenAI, Anthropic's main rival, is also set to debut on the stock market next year.
Both IPOs are taking place amid growing concern about AI and the race to develop AI infrastructure, including data centers that consume vast amounts of energy.
The document filed by Anthropic shows that the company has seen massive revenue growth but is yet to turn a profit, much like its AI rivals.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, the company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30.

And as for money raised at the IPO, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX that ultimately raised $86 billion in what was the biggest IPO on record to date.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is Human Immunodeficiency Virus or HIV?
articles.summary: In recent years, the Philippines has recorded a growing number of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) cases, according to the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP).

blocks.text: In recent years, the Philippines has recorded a growing number of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) cases, according to the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP).
The ASP said HIV in the country can now be considered an epidemic due to the accelerating rate of new infections rather than just the total number of cases.
According to the ASP, the estimated total number of persons living with HIV (PLHIV) as of March 2026 is 288,000.
Meanwhile, the organization reported that by 2030, young people aged 15 to 24 are projected to comprise the majority of HIV cases if proper interventions are not implemented.
HIV is a virus that attacks the body’s immune system, specifically the CD4 cells that help fight off infections and diseases.
But how is it transmitted, and what are the available services in our country to address it?
Transmission
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), HIV is transmitted through infected body fluids such as blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal fluids.
An untreated pregnant mother living with HIV can also pass the virus to her baby during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.
In the Philippines, the ASP reported that 13 cases of mother-to-child HIV transmission (nine male and four female) were recorded from January to March 2026.
ASP president Dr. Rossana Ditangco underscored the importance of universal HIV testing among pregnant women.

“Kaya lahat ng buntis gusto nating ipa-test kasi isa lang buntis ang ma-miss natin diyan, isang bata ‘yan na may new infection. Kaya we are pushing for universal testing of all pregnant women. Kasi ang tolerance natin for mother-to-child transmission is zero,” Ditangco said.

(That is why we want all pregnant women to be tested, because if we miss even just one pregnant mother, that is one child who will contract a new infection. That is why we are pushing for universal testing of all pregnant women—because our tolerance for mother-to-child transmission is zero.)
“... Kasi once tested, the mother can start sa treatment at hindi na niya mai-infect ang kaniyang baby,” she added.
(... Because once tested, the mother can start treatment and will no longer infect her baby.)

Common misconceptions about HIV transmission include beliefs that it spreads through handshakes, toilet seats, swimming pools, kissing, sharing utensils, sneezing, coughing, public spaces and surfaces, sweat, tears, or saliva.
Normalizing HIV Testing
In pushing for better HIV awareness in the country, advocates are aiming to normalize testing first.

The ASP said that having more people consent to HIV testing will help prevent the further rise of HIV cases nationwide—individuals diagnosed with HIV will be provided with appropriate and timely treatment, while those who test negative can be further educated on how to protect themselves.
“Kasi kung normal na ang HIV test, para ka lang nagpa-general checkup, parang nasa package lang ng primary care mo, everybody will get tested nang walang ‘keme’ ika nga,” Ditangco said.
(If HIV testing becomes normalized, it will feel like getting a standard general checkup as part of your primary care package, and everybody will get tested without hesitation.)

According to the APS, the following forms of testing are available in the country and can be accessed free of charge: Rapid Testing, Self-Testing, Community-Based Screening (CBS), and the Rapid HIV Diagnostic Algorithm (rHIVda).
Treatment and prevention
The goal of HIV treatment is to significantly lower the viral level in the body to the point where it can no longer be efficiently transmitted to others.
“Once you start treatment, bababa ‘yung virus sa katawan niya at a very significant level, hindi na siya efficient manghawa ng iba. That’s why treatment is prevention,” Ditangco explained.
(Once you start treatment, the level of the virus in your body drops significantly, making it inefficient for you to infect others. That’s why treatment is prevention.)
This principle is widely known as “U=U,” which stands for “Undetectable equals Untransmittable.”

Under Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), HIV is managed by suppressing viral replication, restoring the immune system, and significantly delaying disease progression by targeting different stages of the HIV life cycle.
According to the ASP, currently available HIV treatments have improved, meaning the virus does not easily develop drug resistance, and patients experience fewer side effects.
The group emphasized that HIV treatment in the Philippines is free under the Outpatient HIV/AIDS Treatment (OHAT) package of PhilHealth.
For prevention, individuals who are potentially exposed to HIV can take pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
PrEP comes in the form of a daily pill or a long-acting injectable taken before potential exposure to the virus. At present, oral PrEP pills are available in the Philippines.
According to Ditangco, injectable PrEP, which is administered once every six months, could soon be available in the Philippines through the Department of Health.

PEP, on the other hand, is taken by an HIV-negative person within 72 hours following a potential exposure to HIV. According to Ditangco, PEP is usually taken during unforeseen events during sexual activity—such as a condom breaking or slipping off.
PEP can also be taken after a needle-stick injury or if an individual shares needles.

Ultimately, the ASP urges a more holistic approach to addressing the HIV epidemic in the Philippines, emphasizing the need for medical assistance alongside mental health support, emotional care, and public education.

Moreover, destigmatizing HIV and supporting persons living with the virus also plays a crucial role in fostering awareness and encouraging more people to seek necessary treatment and support with acceptance rather than fear. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
articles.summary:
Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend

Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK…

blocks.text: Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.
Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.
Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.
It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.

“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.

“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”
She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.

Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.”
In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.

On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.”
Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.

When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”

Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.
“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.”

Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.

Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.

articles.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil
articles.summary:
A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory

After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Brasília and Tom Phillips in São Paulo

blocks.text: After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms.

A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain.

Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.

Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff.
“I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.

Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.
“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná.

Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.
The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.

In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.

Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”.
With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”.

She has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time.

Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m. The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro.

“Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha.

Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.

Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula. We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.”
The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election.
“That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha.
Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”.
“Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added.

items: The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of our Conversations series. Email questions to conversations@theguardian.com

articles.title: Tagle visits hometown, leads celebration of a new parish in Imus, Cavite
articles.summary: Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle made his first trip home after being selected as the Dean of the College of Cardinals and he led the Thanksgiving Mass of a new parish in Imus, Cavite, GMA News' Mariz…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 1:55am

Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle made his first trip home after being selected as the Dean of the College of Cardinals and he led the Thanksgiving Mass of a new parish in Imus, Cavite, GMA News' Mariz Umali reported on "24 Oras."
The Parish of San Roque in Imus, Cavite celebrated its elevation as a parish with Cardinal Tagle leading the thanksgiving activities.
It can be recalled that Tagle was the Bishop of the Diocese of Imus in Cavite for 10 years, before becoming the 32nd Archbishop of Manila. In 2012, Pope Benedict XVI appointed him cardinal.
In 2019, Pope Francis named him prefect of the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples, a key Vatican department responsible for missionary work.

In March 2022, Tagle became pro-prefect of the section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches. The role involved overseeing matters concerning missionary territories and newly established local churches.
In November 2022, Pope Francis replaced Tagle and the leadership of Caritas Internationalis following a Vatican-ordered review that identified deficiencies in management and procedures.
Pope Leo XIV approved the election of Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as dean of the College of Cardinals on October 8, 2026.

Tagle, 69, pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization’s Section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches, succeeds Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, 92, who has held the post since January 2020.
Dean of the College of Cardinals
The Imus native is the first Filipino and Asian cleric selected to lead the elite group that one day will choose Leo's successor.

The College of Cardinals is composed of senior Church leaders who advise the Pope and, when the papacy becomes vacant, elect his successor in a conclave. Only cardinals who meet the requirements under Church law may vote in the papal election.
The Dean serves as the head of the College of Cardinals in a coordinating and representative capacity. The position is often described as primus inter pares, meaning “first among equals.”
Although the Dean does not govern the Church in place of the Pope, the role becomes particularly important when a Pope dies or resigns, and the Church prepares for a new pontificate.
Homily
His homily centered on the celebration of the church's elevation as a parish.
"Biro niyo, ngayon, parokya na ang ating sambayanan... at natutuwa po ako dahil dito sa atin, gumagawa ng bagong parokya," he said.
(Now our community is now a parish... and I'm happy because here among us, a new parish is being built.)
"Sa ibang bahagi ng mundo, nagsasara ang parokya. Alam niyo kung bakit sinasara ang ibang parokya? Wala na kasing pinagpasahan ng pananampalataya," he added.
(In other parts of the world, parishes are closing. Do you know why some parishes are closing? There is no longer any one to pass the faith to.)
The prelate named three actions that San Roque also implemented.

"Una, sa salita ng Diyos. Salita ng Diyos na pinahahayag, pinakikinggan, tinatanggap, sinasapuso, sinasabuhay. ang ikalawa po, ang mga sakramento lalo na ang eukaristiya, ang misa. Patuloy na pinadadaloy ng Panginoon ang kanyang biyaya sa bawat yugto ng ating buhay," Tagle said.

(First, in the word of God. The word of God that is proclaimed, listened to, accepted, taken to heart, and lived. Second, the sacraments, especially the Eucharist and the Mass. The Lord continues to pour out his grace in every stage of our lives.)
The third one he said, "Paglilingkod ng may pag-ibig (Serving with love)."
Cardinal Tagle is staying until Sunday before going to his next mission in Macau. — BAP, GMA News
