articles.title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original Star Trek series, dead at 90
articles.summary: Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the original Star Trek television series and in several movies, has died. He was 90.

image.caption: Walter Koenig, seen here as he was honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Sept. 10, 2012, died Monday at the age of 90, his talent agent said. (David Livingston/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the original Star Trek television series and in several movies, has died. He was 90.
U.S. actor 'was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend,' wrote co-star George Takei
Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighbourhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.

In Star Trek, which ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969, Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the starship Enterprise's bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.
The TV show has also inspired multiple spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.
Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied fierce pride, love of poetry and great loyalty.
"My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate George Takei said in a post on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend."
George Takei as Sulu, left, and Walter Koenig as Chekov are shown in an archival photo from the set of Star Trek: The Original Series. (Getty Images)

"Walter's legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."
McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.
The baby face of the Enterprise
Series creator Gene Roddenberry said Chekov's character, who joined the show in its second season, was a response to Russian complaints about the program.

"They put in Pravda that, 'Ah, the ugly Americans are at it again. They do a space show, and they forget to include the people who were in space first,'" he said, according to The Fifty-Year Mission by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross, an oral history of the Star Trek franchise's first 50 years.
Koenig would become the baby-faced heartthrob of the main cast.

"They wanted somebody who would appeal to eight- to 14-year-olds and the decision was to make him Russian. My fan mail came from eight- to 14-year-olds who weren't that aware of the Cold War and what was going on anyway," Roddenberry told Altman and Gross.
"At the time, the whole thing of getting fan mail was so novel to me that I read every single letter I got. I was literally getting about 700 letters a week, so that took up a lot of my spare time."
Adventure over predictability
Koenig played Chekov in seven Star Trek movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a Star Trek book, Chekov's Enterprise, in 1980.
After Star Trek ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for Family, The Incredible Hulk and other shows. He also taught part-time at UCLA and other schools.

Members of the Star Trek crew (from left): James Doohan, DeForest Kelley, Walter Koenig, William Shatner, George Takei, Leonard Nimoy and Nichelle Nichols toast the then-upcoming film Star Trek V: The Final Frontier during a news conference at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles, Calif., on Dec. 28, 1988. (Bob Galbraith/The Associated Press)
Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a Star Trek theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game Maximum Surge.

"I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option."
He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series Babylon 5.
With files from the CBC's Jonathan Ore and John Mazerolle

articles.title: Judge rules Trump administration illegally fired prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
articles.summary: The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.

image.caption: Maurene Comey, then an assistant U.S. attorney, arrives to a New York City court on May 19, 2025, when she was part of the prosecution team trying Sean (Diddy) Combs. She was fired by the Trump administration weeks later. (Ted Shaffrey/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.
Comey's lawsuit is among a number of wrongful dismissal claims from former Justice Dept., FBI officials

Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the country's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found.

After her firing, Comey sued the U.S. Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.

She asserted she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom U.S. President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.

The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination."

In her lawsuit, Comey asked for the retroactive pay so that she could get back pay and qualify for retirement benefits. In February, she was hired as a partner at New York law firm Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler.
Firing violated constitution, statutes: judge
Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers.
He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
Furman added: "Indeed, to accept defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system."
The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled.
Former FBI director James Comey indicted again over social media post | Hanomansing Tonight
In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said, "The department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."

Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement.
Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
"This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the president is not above the law," they said.

The Justice Department, during the Trump administration, has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.

items: Ex-FBI director Comey's lawyer says government tracked his phone, interviewed mob killer
Gavin Newsom says Trump directed U.S. Justice Department to investigate him

blocks.text: The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.

The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. In the years since, Trump has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.

An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

When James Comey was originally indicted, his son-in-law, Troy Edwards Jr., resigned from his position as assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. He is married to another daughter of Comey's.

The Justice Department and the FBI are facing a number of court challenges related to the ouster of dozens of attorneys and agents who were dismissed after participating in earlier investigations of Trump, or because they were perceived as insufficiently loyal to the Republican president's agenda.
With files from CBC News and Reuters

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leader
articles.summary:
Non-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian rule

Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start…
articles.byline: Jon Henley and Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade

blocks.text: Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, after a seismic weekend election win.

Supporters of the movement, which has no experience of government, took to the streets in the west Balkan country on Monday after the strongman former president, Aleksandar Vučić, was defeated in a historic landslide.

Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday, bringing his domination of Serbian politics to an abrupt end and capping two years of anti-government protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.

With 100% of ballot samples counted, projected results from the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy in Belgrade showed the Student List on 53% of the vote, giving it 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) won 39%, giving it 103. The remaining seats went to national minority party lists.

As yet, there are few clues as to how the winning movement, built around collective decision-making, will actually govern. Its candidates included academics, actors and farmers as well as students, but it is deliberately leaderless with no hierarchy, so it is unclear who it will appoint as the prime minister and cabinet.

Prominent Student List figures include: ​Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who headed the candidate list; Dejan Šoškić, a former central bank governor; and Radomir Saičić, a chemistry professor at Belgrade ​University who spoke on behalf ‌of the List after its ​victory.

Much like Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years of illiberal government in Hungary this spring, the List faces public institutions staffed with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime, complicating the task of institutional overhaul.

“Everyone in the student movement, and every candidate on the list, has a complete and very clear understanding of the weight of the responsibility before us,” said Ana Mirković, a university educationist, psychologist and Student List candidate.
“We do not see the election result as gaining power and privileges, but as taking on a historic debt to our own people and to our own children.”
Mirković told the Guardian the movement’s first priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Vučić’s 14-year rule has been described as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending control over the media, judiciary and other state institutions and elections marred by registration irregularities, media bias and voter bribes.

The students’ platform centres on a pledge to fight corruption and restore the rule of law, including creating an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, not the interior ministry, and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime.

blocks.caption: Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP

blocks.text: It also aims to ban appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies and to promote financial accountability and public scrutiny – by new independent bodies – of all major state infrastructure contracts ⁠to curb the misuse of public funds.

Mirković said the new government would dismantle a “system of intimidation” that encouraged “fear and polarisation”, by “urgently opening up” the media, putting an end to pressure on public-sector workers and “stopping institutional violence”.

She added that the aim was to “rebuild society from the ground up: full disclosure of all contracts and financial flows; depoliticising and strengthening the judiciary; renewing the education and healthcare systems”, and that state capture should “never again” be possible.

The Student List deliberately kept divisive foreign policy issues, including relations with the EU and Russia, in the background. The Kremlin said on Monday it hoped the new leaders “understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests”.
after newsletter promotion

Dušan Vučićević, an analyst, said that, from the outset, the movement “insisted as much as possible that Serbia must first and foremost address domestic political issues – the literal dismantling of every institution, from the national to the local level”.

The students’ win marks a profound political shift in Serbia and could potentially offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.

However, Vučićević said it was distinct from other protests. “This experiment in grassroots democracy ultimately secured more than 50% of the vote,” he told Agence France-Presse, but it was “unclear whether a similar model could work in other countries”.

Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based Centre for Contemporary Politics, said on Monday that the movement’s decision-making process also needed to “be sped up”, as its process for choosing candidates “actually took a long time – months”.

He added: “After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. Twenty-four hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy.”

On Sunday, Vučić, who maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed his party’s defeat on “the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump”.

International leaders, meanwhile, joined a chorus of welcome to the students on Monday. “This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“We wish ⁠Serbia success, real development, and warm ⁠relations with the European community. ​We in Ukraine thank Serbia for respecting our people, our state, and our independence. And we always celebrate our shared achievements.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Berlin would “actively support Serbia’s European path” after the victory, saying the students “with their demand for the rule of law, fighting corruption and fundamental freedoms, have reached the people”.
Serbia’s constitution requires the new parliament to convene within 30 days of the official election result, and sets a 90-day deadline after that for formation of the new government.
The country must also hold new presidential elections before 27 December, since Vučić stepped down to run for prime minister.

articles.title: Brazil runoff as it happened: world leaders congratulate Lula on historic election win as Bolsonaro refuses to concede
articles.summary: Leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated the far-right senator and was elected president of Brazil for a fourth non-consecutive term
articles.byline: Tom Ambrose (now); Martin Belam, Yohannes Lowe, Adam Fulton and Marina Dunbar (earlier)

blocks.text: What you need to know about the historic Brazilian election vote

It has just gone past 06:15am in Brasília and 09:15am in London, where I am blogging from. Here is a quick recap of the main updates from one of the most significant and bruising elections in Brazilian history:

items: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election comeback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
Lula secured 51.79% of the votes compared with Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court – about 4.4m more votes
Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept the election result, and has called for it to be annulled.
The 45-year-old senator called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed supreme court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities.

His refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the supreme court to 27-years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.
Lula, who highlighted a track record of falling poverty and inequality during his campaign, becomes the first president in Brazilian history to win a fourth term.

It is also the first time, since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1988, that a candidate who lost the first round of voting went on to overturn the result and win the presidency. Lula’s new term is set to begin on 5 January 2027.
The leftist president’s victory is a blow for the US president, who had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in South America.
Numerous world leaders have congratulated Lula for his dramatic election win, but so far Donald Trump has remained silent.

blocks.text: You can read more in this insightful recap from my colleagues, Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero:

blocks.text: Closing summary

items: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro. “This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff. Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

However, Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

The scale of Bolsonaro’s loss, with the senator trailing Lula by over 4 ​million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. Less than ‌35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, ‌were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.

Political leaders and governments from across the spectrum were quick to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”

French president Emmanuel Macron said France and Brazil had “much to build together,” while European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said “democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.” The Kremlin welcomed Lula’s re-election and praised him for his contribution ‌to bilateral ties and to BRICS. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy congratulated the leftist leader on “remarkable election results” and said he looked forward to expanding cooperation.

Rampant selling tore through financial markets at the shock result, as investors reversed positions that had largely been built around expectations of a Bolsonaro victory. Brazil’s currency tumbled over 11% against the US dollar in early spot trading, one of its biggest daily declines on record, while the benchmark Bovespa stock ⁠index was down more than 15% in its largest daily percentage drop since 1998.

blocks.text: Nearly three million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.
Here is a graphic that shows how that compares with previous elections in the country:

blocks.caption: Tiago Rogero

blocks.text: Tiago Rogero

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo published an analysis showing that only 34,330 votes, or 0.03% of the total, were cast after the original 5pm closing time, an insignificant number compared with the 4.4 million-vote margin by which president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his opponent.

The decision to extend voting until 7pm so that voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport could cast their ballots is at the heart of far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s attempt to have the election annulled.

However, the president of the electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, has already said the extension did not affect the result and, like the leaders of other Brazilian institutions including the supreme court and congress, has recognised Lula’s re-election.

So few votes were actually cast because, as the decision to extend voting hours came minutes after 5pm, the vast majority of electronic voting machines had already been closed and could not be reopened.

The analysis was carried out at Folha de S.Paulo’s request by data journalist and university professor Pedro Burgos, who believes most of the 34,000 votes cast after 5pm were from voters who were already queuing when the original voting period ended – meaning they would have been able to vote even without the extension.
The British foreign secretary has described Lula’s victory as “a historic win for the global progressive movement” as he offered his congratulations.
Ed Miliband wrote on X:

double quotation markCongratulations to @LulaOficial on his re-election. Together, our two governments have promoted shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action since 2024 and look forward to continuing to do so. His victory is a historic win for the global progressive movement.

We reported earlier that the Kremlin had sent a warm message to Lula on his re-election, with Valdimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying it was “welcomed”, praising his efforts on the “development of bilateral relations” between the two nations.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also commented. He said:

double quotation markFor us in Ukraine, it is important that Brazil remains active in international affairs and continues to contribute to the effective protection of human rights, the rights of peoples, and the rights of states. We thank Brazil for its unwavering support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We look forward to expanding our cooperation.

Dr Marco Vieira, associate professor in international relations at the University of Birmingham in England, has said there are three distinct reasons why the world should pay attention to the election result in Brazil. He said:

double quotation markFirst, Lula’s victory reinforces Brazil’s role in spearheading efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest, with clear implications for global climate patterns, food production and the rights of Indigenous populations living in the region. Second, Lula will now face a major challenge as the leader of South America’s largest economy and one of the region’s most important powers resisting what Trump has called his “Donroe Doctrine”, a policy of expanding US influence and asserting US dominance in the western Hemisphere. Third, Brazil is likely to continue its international activism through forums such as BRICS and the G20, positioning itself as a leading voice in debates over global governance reform and the defence of multilateral institutions. In a context of growing global uncertainty, the certainty of Lula leading Brazil for the next four years provides an important source of support for other middle powers seeking to rebuild trust in multilateralism and peaceful cooperation.

blocks.caption: Tom Phillips

blocks.text: Tom Phillips
Tom Phillips is the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent
I’ve been speaking to Brazil’s former environment minister, the world-renowned environmentalist Marina Silva, here in São Paulo.

A few days ago she told me that if Flávio Bolsonaro were to be elected president he would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rampant rainforest destruction initiated by his jailed far-right father.
On Sunday night Silva was in a far more upbeat mood as she arrived at the hall where Lula was celebrating his election triumph with hundreds of ecstatic supporters.
“My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people,” she told me.

“The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations,” Silva said.

blocks.caption: Brazil's former minister of the environment Marina Silva. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Jair Bolsonaro spent his 2019-22 presidency stripping away environmental and Indigenous protests and was nicknamed “Captain Chainsaw” because of the devastation inflicted on the environment under his watch.

After beating Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, Lula launched a major crackdown to evict illegal miners from Indigenous lands and a broader environmental offensive across the Amazon that cut deforestation to its lowest levels since the late 80s.
Those efforts will now continue.
Summary of the day so far …

items: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
However, soon after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled.

Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.

His claim apears to be making little headway, with president of the electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, and the heads of the supreme court, the lower house and the senate all recognising the result and congratulating the incumbent on his re-election.

The unexpected result has caused some market turmoil, with Brazil’s National Treasury cancelling ⁠auctions of inflation-linked ⁠and fixed-rate government ​bonds, the São Paulo stock exchange halting trading, and Brazil’s real weakened ⁠12.2% ⁠against ​the US ⁠dollar.

The Kremlin has welcomed Lula’s election victory, saying the leftist president had done “a lot” to develop ties with Russia. Numerous other world leaders have congratulated Lula for his dramatic election win, but so far Donald Trump has remained silent.
You can find the full election results here.

Brazil’s National Treasury said in ⁠a ⁠statement on ​Monday it has canceled ⁠the conventional auctions of inflation-linked ⁠and fixed-rate government ​bonds scheduled ‌for ‌27 October and ‌29 October, Reuters reports.
Reuters reports that the currency market speculators have had their say on the election result – Brazil’s real weakened ⁠12.2% ⁠against ​the US ⁠dollar in spot trading ⁠early ​on Monday.

articles.title: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
articles.summary: The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.

blocks.text: Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.
The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.

Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.

Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.
However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.
The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.
"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.

Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.
Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.
Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.

Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

articles.title: German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
articles.summary: A three-ship collision has led to the cancellation of a cruise and expensive damages. Shipyard repairs are needed, and further cruises could be affected.

image.caption: Police are investigating whether the captain breached his duty of care during the ship's departureImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.
The collision caused damage estimated to be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.
Why are police investigating the captain?

A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.
Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.
How did the collision happen?
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.
The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.
The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.

blocks.caption: The collision forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with police investigating the captainImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.
Could more cruises be canceled?
Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.

The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.
It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.
The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

articles.title: Drug, roadworthiness tests at bus terminals as PH readies for Undas 2026
articles.summary: Authorities carried out drug and alcohol tests on provincial bus drivers and tested buses for roadworthiness at several terminals in Metro Manila ahead of Undas 2026.

blocks.text: Authorities carried out drug and alcohol tests on provincial bus drivers and tested buses for roadworthiness at several terminals in Metro Manila ahead of the expected deluge of passengers leaving town for Undas 2026.
With a few days to go before the Undas properly begins at the weekend, many people are already at the bus terminals, having decided to leave to beat the bulk of the holiday rush.
In Mark Salazar's report on Saksi on Monday, Samantha Pilapil was among the passengers waiting to board the bus to Masbate at a terminal in Cubao, Quezon City.
"Kaya ako bumiyahe nang maaga kasi ayoko pong makisiksik sa maraming tao," she said, cradling one-year-old child on her lap.
(I'm traveling early because I don't want to squeeze in with the crowds.)
Some buses were also stopped from traveling due to deficiencies, with passengers having to disembark to move to another bus.
"Ilang lipat na po kami, sobra nang init ng panahon," one complained.
(We've had to move so many times, and it's so hot.)

According to the Land Transportation Office (LTO), 51 out of 52 passenger buses passed the roadworthiness inspection conducted at the terminals in Manila, Parañaque and Caloocan City. The lone failure didn't pass due to a broken reverse light and plate light, and an expired fire extinguisher. The driver was instructed to have the defects repaired and the expired fire extinguisher replaced before traveling again.
Drug, alcohol tests
None of the bus drivers tested positive for alcohol, the authorities said after conducting breathalyzer tests. However, there were some positive drug tests.

"After the field tests and the result yielded positive, ikinukumpiska natin yung [we confiscate the] driver's license, at yung person na nag-positive sa drug test will be subjected to rehabilitation" said retired Police Brigadier General Allan Nobleza of the LTO law enforcement service.
At the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX), there were no positive alcohol tests but one positive drug test.

"Out of 85 so far na tinest po natin na mga drivers, may nag-positive pong isa," said Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) Chair Don Artes. "So kinausap po namin siya ni RD Carreon kanina, at itinanggi po niya na siya po ay gumamit ng droga. So isa-subject po iyan sa confirmatory test...kasi minsan daw lalo na pag may iniinom na gamot na certain types of medicine, nagre-react yung test kit, that's why we have to have a confirmatory test."

(Out of 85 so far tested, one has tested positive. We talked to him and he denied using drugs. So he will undergo a confirmatory test, because sometimes the test kits may react to certain types of medicine, that's why we have to have a confirmatory test.)

"Pag na-rule out talaga na hindi droga ang nag-trigger ng [If illegal drugs are ruled out as the reason for the] presumptive positive result, then by all means his license will be released back to him and he will be allowed to travel," added Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency-National Capital Region (PDEA-NCR) Regional Director Derrick Carreon.
The PITX is expecting a passenger volume of 1.8 million in the period from October 31 to November 3.

"This is not as high as expected, kasi nakita natin this time meron tayong isa pang long weekend na ina-anticipate, which is the ASEAN long weekend," said PITX spokesperson Jason Salvador. "So baka naman yung iba sa kababayan natin hindi na makikipag-sabayan sa rush ngayon and piliin nilang umuwi sa kanilang mga probinsiya sa ASEAN holiday."

(This is not as high as expected, because this time we have another long weekend, the ASEAN long weekend. So maybe some of our compatriots have decided not to deal with the Undas rush and instead go home for the ASEAN holiday.)
November 16, 17 and 18 have been declared special non-working days in the National Capital Region in connection with the country's hosting of the ASEAN and related summits.
NAIA preps

Meanwhile, the country's gateway NAIA is preparing for an estimated 1.25 million passengers during the Undas travel period from Oct. 27 to Nov. 4, with airport authorities projecting Oct. 30 to be the busiest day.

In a news release, New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC), the airport operator, said it expects passenger traffic during the nine-day period to increase by 1% from the 1.24 million recorded during the same period last year. About 149,000 travelers are expected to pass through the airport on Oct. 30 alone.

To manage the holiday rush, NNIC said it would deploy additional personnel, strengthen security and passenger assistance services, and maintain round-the-clock monitoring of airport operations. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Serbia wakes up to new reality after student-led movement ousts Vučić – as it hapepned
articles.summary: Hopes raised for a reset in relations with EU and other partners following the defeat of authoritarian president

blocks.text: Morning opening: Serbia wakes up to new reality after Vučić

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Serbia wakes up to a new reality this morning after a grassroots opposition movement led by students ousted the country’s former authoritarian president Aleksandar Vučić, raising hopes for a new opening in relations with the EU and other partners.

blocks.caption: Opposition supporters celebrate at the parliament building after Aleksandar Vučić, represented by the silhouette, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

blocks.text: With 96.9% polling stations processed, the Student List has 52.6% of votes, well ahead of Vučić’s bloc at 39.22%.

The latest CeSID projection suggested the students will have 140 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority, with 103 for Vucic’s bloc. No other party crossed the 3% threshold, with national minority parties taking the remaining seven seats.
We are likely to get more reactions to the vote today, with international observers set to present their preliminary report on the vote in the early afternoon.
I will also pick up the latest on the first round of the presidential vote in Bulgaria, which saw a record-low turnout of just 22%. The second round will be held this Sunday.

Elsewhere, I will be looking for updates from France and Italy after another rocky weekend of protests. French PM Sébastien Lecornu is going to meet with the student unions in the afternoon for what could be pivotal talks on the future of the demonstrations.

And E5 defence ministers – that’s France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK – are meeting in Paris for discussions on Ukraine. Oh, and Slovakia’s foreign minister Juraj Blanár is in Moscow for energy talks with Russia.
It’s Monday, 26 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

items: International observers issued an overall positive assessment of the Serbian election, despite major underlying structural issues on state capture, polarisation, and misuse of state resources that require urgent addressing in the future (15:10, 15:15, 15:19, 15:37, 15:54)
The largest domestic group of observers also urged the incoming new government to “re-establish the integrity of elections” as one of its top priorities (13:31).
The focus now shifts to the government formation process as we wait for the official results to kick off the constitutional timeline (16:31).

Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić is seen as a possible future prime minister, but the consultative and decentralised nature of the student movement makes it tricky to pinpoint who will get the top job (17:17).
Several EU leaders offered their congratulations for the student movement as they hoped for renewed engagement between the EU and Serbia (10:21, 12:15).
Russia said it hoped for cooperation with the new Serbian authorities, despite their preferred candidate Aleksandar Vučić losing the election (11:18).

items: In France, it is make or break time for the government on high school protests, which continued over the weekend, with the government now expected to set out new proposals to address the key demands in the late afternoon (13:02).
Bulgaria will head to the polls this Sunday in a runoff of the presidential race, with the list of candidates narrowed to two main favourites (12:59).

How to choose your grassroots prime minister?
One thing to watch out for is how the Student List will pick its top figures, including the next prime minister and their presidential candidate.

blocks.caption: An empty prime ministerial lectern at the Student List headquarters, as the screen displays a message which reads “Serbia is Free”. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the key features of the movement so far is that everything has been covered by very extensive and time-consuming consultations with student plenum meetings across the country, including the vetting of all candidates on the electoral list.

That may, of course, not always be possible in the future given the urgency some decisions will demand. The students will quickly need to figure out how to streamline these decision-making processes and make them work at the pace governing demands.

It may be easier to run a similarly complex process to choose their presidential candidate, as there is still some time to go until the vote in late December, but less so when it comes to the top jobs in the government, starting from the prime minister, and his key ministers.

“There is almost certainly going to be a complex process. It will not be decided by a small group of people sitting somewhere in a room. It’s only a matter of how complicated it will be,” Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based thinktank Centre for Contemporary Politics explained.

“It will have to be sped up because the process of choosing candidates for the list actually took a long time, months, to finish … [and finished] literally one day before they submitted the list. So, it has to be shorter.”
And the constitutional deadlines (16:31) will “force them to choose their candidates more quickly,” Aleksandar Ivković, a researcher at the Centre for Contemporary Politics added.

Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić, who in 2012 resigned two years into the job in protest against alleged interference with his independence, is widely seen as the frontrunner for the job of the prime minister, but let’s see what other names can come up and who can emerged unscathed through the vetting process.

“After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. 24 hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy to us,” Burazer said.

blocks.caption: People celebrate outside the National Assembly in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Armin Durgut/AP

blocks.text: What's next in Serbia - timeline
In terms of next steps in Serbia, here is what we know for now.

We are still waiting for the final election results: more than 97% polling station are now counted, but there are some localised issues that may even, in extreme cases, prompt a revote in some individual polling stations.
None of this will affect the overall result, but may cause a delay of a week or two from today.

blocks.caption: A voter prepares to cast a ballot at a polling station for Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections in Niš, southern Serbia. Photograph: Sasa Djordjevic/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Once the results are published, the National Assembly needs to meet for the first time within 30 days – that gets us to early to mid-December at the latest – starting the 90 days deadline for forming the new government.

This in itself will be fascinating as we have no idea who could emerge as the next prime minister given the leaderless nature of the Student List. Expect lots of speculation on this in the coming weeks, with former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić often mentioned as a possible candidate.

blocks.caption: Former national bank governor Dejan Šoškić is the Student List MP with most experience of running public institutions. Could he be the next prime minister? Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/Reuters

blocks.text: It’s worth saying that given the Student List will have a majority in the new parliament, they are very unlikely to need to run the clock down, and so the process can be well accelerated: many experts expect the new government to take over in December at the latest.

That timing is convenient for one more reason: following Vučić’s resignation as president to run for parliament, Serbia must hold a presidential election to choose a new head of state before the end of the year (well, by 27 December).

A close Vučić ally, Ana Brbabić, is currently the acting president as the last speaker of the parliament. Once we have a new speaker – presumably from the Student List – he or she will take over that interim role from here until the new leader gets elected.
That should make for an exciting end to the year in Serbia, with all change at the top going into 2027.
Serbian election marred by 'grave misuse of public resources' and 'intimidation of voters,' observers say
The preliminary report from international observers is also now out in writing, if you fancy reading it in full.

“Serbia’s 25 October early parliamentary elections saw active citizen engagement, with high voter turnout and vigorous competition between two main contenders, but unfolded in an atmosphere of profound polarisation, with equality of campaign opportunities seriously compromised, international observers said in a preliminary statement released today. Entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party, including the grave misuse of public resources, together with intimidation and pressure on voters, alongside disruptions of campaign activities, further marred the electoral environment, the statement says.”
The report is here.
International observers warn of issues with social media's impact on elections
Ireland’s Eoghan Murphy, who heads the ODIHR’s mission, goes into much more detail than other politicians on various technical issues in Serbia.

He talks in detail about the abuse of state resources for campaigning purposes, instances of intimidation and confrontation during the campaign, and serious issues spotted on social media and in traditional media.
This last point is particularly relevant as it feels it could just as well apply to most countries with elections coming up.
He warns that online campaigning “remains largely unregulated,” with “no dedicated oversight mechanism, safeguards … or accountability.”
“We don’t know how social media platforms prioritise and amplify such content, which harms transparency, and this reinforces the need for oversight and for safeguards.”
Sounds familiar?

He also makes it very clear that Serbia’s state media were way too involved in the election, with “pronounced imbalances in exposure and treatment of contestants, contrary to its legal obligations and public service mandate.”
“Overall, most monitored broadcasters failed to provide voters with the substantive and impartial information necessary to make an informed choice.”
Italian MP Federica Onori, for the OSCE PA delegation, talks about the problems with diaspora vote, which saw people stand in endless queues, including in London.

“The arrangements for voting abroad raised concerns about the disproportionate inconvenience of voters in certain countries due to the absence of clear and objective criteria regarding polling stations, locations, and voting hours.”
Austrian MEP Andreas Schieder, head of the European parliament’s mission, also flags this problem, and says “this needs to change in the future.”

blocks.caption: Serbian voters around the world queue to cast ballots in snap parliamentary election

blocks.text: Italian MP Pierro Fassino, head of the parliamentary assembly of Council of Europe’s delegation and an Italian MP in his own right, is up next.
He says the election took place in a “calm and responsible manner … despite the polarised” atmosphere, with the electoral process passing the assessment at 96% of the polling stations observed.
The press conference continues along these lines, so I will flag if anyone disagrees with this view – or say anything particularly exciting about their experience of monitoring the vote.
International observers conclude with preliminary 'positive' assessment of Serbia vote, despite major structural issues
Special coordinator and Luxembourgish MP Gilles Baum is now speaking at the presentation of the international observers’ preliminary verdict on the election.

He says the election “unfolded in the atmosphere of profound polarisation, with the equality of campaign opportunity seriously compromised” through “entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party.”
He also talks about the suspected “misuse of state resources together with intimidation and pressure on voters, candidates and civil society, as well as disruption of campaign activities.”
He warns that despite previous recommendations, “widespread distrust in the integrity of the voter registration persisted.”
But the mission’s on the day observation concludes with “positive” assessment of all stages of the election day process “in the vast majority of polling stations observer.”
“Nevertheless, reported incidents of physical violence raised serious concerns, and some procedural shortcomings were noted,” he says.

The main group of international observers – including OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the European parliament - is about to deliver their preliminary verdict on the Serbian election, with a press conference in Belgrade.
I will keep an eye on this and bring you the key lines.
Most of the student list’s 250 candidates were experts from fields including academia and the arts with little political experience.

We are still waiting for the official confirmation of the exact names that will sit in the new parliament, but given their roots in academia they may very well have a chance to be among the best educated parliamentary caucuses in Europe. More than 160 of the 250 candidates held a PhD!
(But, perhaps a little-known fact, none of them were actually students; they were picked by students.)
As explained yesterday, the movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.
It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.
The movement deliberately kept foreign policy issues, including Serbia’s relationship with the European Union and longtime ally Russia, in the background.
‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat
Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade and Ashifa Kassam

Standing on the streets of Belgrade, as passing cars honked excitedly and revellers high-fived police officers, Sara, 24, gestures to the streets around her to explain just how much things had changed for Serbia’s student-led movement.

blocks.caption: Sara, 24, centre, celebrates the opposition election win in Belgrade, Serbia, flanked by her friends Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The Guardian

blocks.text: Moments earlier, the country’s longstanding leader, Aleksandar Vučić, had conceded defeat to the student movement, ushering in a seismic political shift in the Balkan country.
It was a surreal reversal of fortunes for the hundreds of thousands of people who had spent nearly two years peacefully protesting against a ruling power that had become increasingly authoritarian.
“It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors.”
If you want to catch up with last night’s wild celebrations in Belgrade, here are two quick videos for you to get an idea of what the party atmosphere on the streets of the capital was like.

CRTA’s Raša Nedeljkov is currently presenting the organisation’s preliminary findings on last night’s elections, with a long list of reasons and issues that essentially make the Student List’s win against the incumbents even more impressive.

blocks.caption: A drone view shows people queueing outside a polling station to vote during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

blocks.text: He says that “systemic manipulation at the polling stations was largely prevented” by the record-high number of domestic observers – up to 15,000, three times more than in 2023 – and usual citizens getting involved in running polling stations.
He says international observers also played a role in the process, but they had a “different role,” without permanent structures in place to observe broader, systemic abuses.

Summing up yesterday’s vote, he says there were still clear issues with voter identification, the use of UV lamps (we explained what they use them for yesterday), and how polling stations were set up, and calls for an urgent reform of the system.

“Re-establishing the integrity of elections should be among the top priorities of the new legislative and executive authority and seen as the foundation for the recovery of democratic institutions in Serbia,” he said.

“Serbia should never again participate in elections that … were marked by the misuse of state and public resources,” he said, with “significant efforts to bring the flow of information under the total control of the government,” with attacks on media and social media as well as attempts to discredit election observers.
He says that he still believes the state capture by Vučić’s ruling party influenced the result of the election, given voter intimidation and state-media propaganda.

“You had one political leader [Vučić] who had public addresses in our media more than 500 times, on camera, live, on average 30 minutes. Give me a country in the world, except North Korea, that has this kind of [single-party] dominance in the media.”

articles.title: More than 60 Christians killed in Ethiopia 'massacre', church official says
articles.summary: One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush, saying they were surrounded.

blocks.text: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.

One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic.
The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible.

A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks.
A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible.
Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children.
A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault.
Many residents have now fled the area.

Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence".

In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution".
The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years.
But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period.
The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks.

The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country.
The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations.
Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.
About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim.

articles.title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
articles.summary: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
By
Diplomatic correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

blocks.caption: James Landale

blocks.text: In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.
Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.
The Iran question
The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.
He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.
His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.
'Legacy mode'

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.
"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

blocks.text: Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.
Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".
It's the economy

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

blocks.text: Image source, Chris Torres / EPA/Shutterstock
Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

blocks.text: Image source, Abir Sultan Credit / EPA/Shutterstock
The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.
Top image credit: Getty.
